01 / SCALEGraduate research · 2025—2026

A soft interface
for self-care
in public.

SCALE explores how a treatment aid can reduce hand contact, protect irritated skin and feel socially acceptable in everyday situations.

Role
Independent researcher and designer
Methods
Semi-structured interviews, open coding, journey mapping, Kano, Better–Worse
Output
30 UX requirements, three form prototypes, use scenarios
Scope
Experience and form exploration; not a clinical device study

The project began with a simple contradiction: people need to respond quickly to discomfort, yet the act of applying treatment can feel messy, visible and disruptive.

01Context

Why treatment is delayed in public settings.

Literature and user accounts pointed to recurring friction around hand contamination, exposing the affected area, residue after application and the attention of people nearby.

I reframed the brief from “a better applicator” to “a discreet layer that helps treatment fit into the flow of everyday life.”

02Research

Interviews, open coding and Kano prioritization.

23semi-structured interviews
30experience requirements after open coding
367valid responses from 400 Kano surveys
Listen

Behavior in context

Participants described when they apply, delay or avoid treatment and what makes the action uncomfortable.

Structure

Open coding

Interview material was grouped into thirty experience requirements spanning safety, usability, feedback and emotional acceptance.

Prioritize

Kano + Better–Worse

A quantitative survey clarified which requirements most strongly shaped confidence and continued use.

Coefficient calculation

Turning Kano responses into comparable priorities.

The Better coefficient estimates the potential gain in satisfaction when a need is fulfilled. The negative Worse coefficient indicates the risk of dissatisfaction when it is unmet.

Betteri = Ai + OiAi + Oi + Mi + Ii
Worsei = − Oi + MiAi + Oi + Mi + Ii

A · AttractiveO · One-dimensionalM · Must-beI · Indifferent

03Priority

Safety and treatment confidence ranked highest.

The composite priority scores moved the design away from appearance-led decisions. Safety, confidence and simple operation became the first filters for every concept.

01Safety & reliability0.76
02Trust in treatment0.73
03Simple operation0.71
04Clear feedback0.70
05Ease of understanding0.70
EvidenceDesign decision

Hand contaminationSeparate the treatment area from the touch area.

Social hesitationUse a soft, non-clinical visual language.

Movement and body curvatureDevelop three structures instead of forcing one universal form.

04Translation

One visual language, three body contexts.

Protective shells, thin wing membranes and segmented bodies offered structural references for coverage, flexibility and movement. The biological cues were abstracted rather than copied literally.

A

Shield

Broad curved coverage for the back, chest and thigh.

B

Joint Scale

A segmented radial structure for shoulders, elbows and knees.

C

Flat Patch

A compact form for the jawline and smaller body folds.

05Prototype

Thermochromic feedback without a digital display.

Low-hardness Ecoflex silicone supported the exploratory goal of close contact and movement. Moulds were produced for three forms and tested through physical making.

Thermochromic pigment activated around 31°C was explored as gentle, non-diagnostic feedback. The study did not validate clinical efficacy, biocompatibility or long-term hygiene.

06Scenario

Prepared before leaving. Applied when needed.

A six-step scenario examined the flow from preparing and carrying the patch to applying it during transit and storing it after use.

Reflection

The research produced a defensible direction, not a finished medical claim.

The next stage would require controlled usability testing, skin-contact safety verification, cleaning studies and collaboration with clinical specialists.
